title: The 55-25-20 Portfolio: How Adding Equity and Gold to Debt Nearly Doubled Returns Over 25 Years
excerpt: A WhiteOak Capital study of rolling returns from 2001 to 2026 finds that mixing debt, equity, and gold can boost returns by 5 percentage points with barely any extra volatility.
body:
• A portfolio of 55% debt, 25% equity, and 20% gold delivered 11.60% average annual returns with volatility barely above a 100% debt portfolio's 6.38%, according to a WhiteOak Capital study spanning September 2001 to June 2026
  • Adding just 10% equity to a pure debt portfolio improved returns from 6.79% to 7.99% while actually reducing volatility from 6.38% to 5.76%
  • A separate Funds India study found a 70% equity, 15% debt, 15% gold portfolio delivered above 10% returns in 92% of seven-year periods since 2000
  • The highest-returning combination was 10% debt, 70% equity, and 20% gold at 17.02% annually, but with significantly higher volatility at 17.28%

The Core Finding

Investors often assume that adding equity to a portfolio automatically increases risk. A 25-year analysis by WhiteOak Capital Mutual Fund challenges that assumption with data spanning from September 2001 to June 2026.

The study, reported by Livemint, analysed rolling one-year returns using the Crisil 10 Year Gilt Index for debt, the BSE Sensex TRI for equity, and MCX Gold in INR. The central finding: a 100% debt portfolio delivered an average annual return of 6.79% with 6.38% volatility. But adding 10% equity brought returns up to 7.99% while volatility actually fell to 5.76%—a counterintuitive result driven by the low correlation between asset classes.

"Adding a judicious combination of low, negligible and negatively correlated asset classes can help improve the risk-adjusted return profile of a portfolio."

— WhiteOak Capital Mutual Fund Study

The Sweet Spot: Debt-Equity-Gold Combinations

When gold enters the picture as a third asset class, the risk-return dynamics improve further. A portfolio with 55% debt, 25% equity, and 20% gold delivered an average annual return of 11.60%—nearly 5 percentage points above the pure debt portfolio—while maintaining broadly similar volatility.

The lowest-volatility combination among all options tested was 70% debt, 10% equity, and 20% gold, which delivered 9.79% average annual returns with just 5.52% volatility. For investors seeking the highest returns, 10% debt, 70% equity, and 20% gold generated 17.02% annually, though volatility climbed to 17.28%.

Corroboration From a Second Study

A separate report by investment platform Funds India, analysed by Outlook Money, arrived at complementary conclusions. Their study found that a portfolio with 70% equity, 15% debt, and 15% gold delivered returns above 10% in 92% of all seven-year periods between January 2000 and February 2026. The average annual return for this allocation was approximately 15.10%, with the worst seven-year period still returning about 7%.

The Funds India analysis used the Nifty 50 TRI for equity, low-duration and corporate bond funds for debt, and rupee-denominated gold prices. Portfolios were assumed to be rebalanced annually whenever allocations deviated by more than five percentage points.

What the Numbers Mean in Practice

For an 80% debt and 20% equity portfolio, the average annual return was 9.20% at the same volatility as 100% debt. Moving to 75-25 debt-equity added another 60 basis points in returns with only a marginal volatility increase. At the other extreme, 100% equity generated the highest average return of 18.82% but came with the highest volatility of 25.35%.

The study's practical implication is straightforward: most investors can improve their risk-adjusted returns by holding a mix of all three asset classes rather than concentrating in any single one. The exact ratio depends on individual risk tolerance and investment horizon.

Portfolio Guidance by Age

Industry experts generally recommend adjusting allocations as investors age. A 25-year-old with a long investment horizon might hold 80% equity, 10% debt, and 10% gold. A 45-year-old in peak earning years could target 60% equity, 30% debt, and 10% gold. For a 65-year-old retiree, the focus shifts toward 20-25% equity, 60-70% debt, and 5-10% gold, according to expert commentary compiled by Livemint.

Across all age groups, financial advisors emphasise annual portfolio reviews and periodic rebalancing to maintain target allocations—a process that has historically captured gains from asset classes that have outperformed while systematically buying into those that have underperformed.
